NARRATIVE: on october 22, 2024, during routine pigging of a 30-inch, api 5l x70 steel transmission line operating at 1150 psig, the pig became lodged near a 12-inch reduction valve at milepost 57. after attempts to retrieve the pig with a push-through tool failed, the control system automatically opened the downstream emergency shut-off valve, causing a pressure surge that exceeded the valve's set-point of 1200 psig. the surge resulted in a short-duration vent of approximately 350 scfd through the vent stack before the valve closed. the vent was detected by the remote monitoring system, and operators initiated an emergency response. a subsequent inspection revealed that a corrosion-induced wall thinning of the reduction valve body had reduced its structural integrity, allowing the over-pressure condition. the valve was replaced, the affected pipeline segment was hydrostatically tested to 1300 psig, and normal service was restored after a 48-hour outage. no injuries or third-party damage were reported, and the incident was logged with the ferc and state pipeline safety board for further review.

NARRATIVE: on 9/14/2023 at 08:45 a.m. field crews observed a faint hissing sound near milepost 212+30 on the 30-in. api 5l x70 steel line (design pressure 1 200 psi) transporting sweet natural gas at 980 psi. initial visual inspection revealed a small, wet area on the north side of the right-hand side girth weld, but no obvious puncture. a portable gas detector confirmed elevated methane concentrations (12 % vol) at the site. the line was immediately isolated by closing the upstream block valve at station 212+45 and the downstream valve at station 212+15, reducing pressure to 150 psi to prevent further release. maintenance personnel erected a temporary containment dome and began depressurizing the isolated segment. after 30 minutes the pressure dropped to 45 psi and the hissing ceased. excavation uncovered a hairline crack, ~0.8 in. long, propagating through the weld throat. metallurgical analysis later indicated the crack originated from an incomplete fusion defect left from the original fabrication, which was aggravated by cyclic pressure fluctuations during peak demand periods. the compromised section was cut out and a new 30-in. spool with full-penetration welds was installed. post-repair hydrostatic testing was performed at 1 200 psi for 30 minutes with no leaks detected. the line was returned to service at 09:30 a.m. on 9/15/2023.

NARRATIVE: on august 14, at approximately 0930 hrs, a residential contractor was excavating a backyard for a new septic tank on county road 12, near milepost 27.5. while using a compact excavator, the operator struck a 24-in. carbon-steel natural gas transmission pipe (api 5l grade b) buried at a depth of 4 ft. the pipe, part of the central valley mainline, was operating at 900 psig and transporting dry natural gas at a flow rate of 1.2 mmcf/d. the impact caused a 3-in. longitudinal gouge, resulting in an immediate gas release. nearby residents reported a strong odor of natural gas. the contractor halted work and called emergency services; the utility's emergency response team arrived at 0945 hrs and initiated an emergency shutdown by closing the upstream and downstream isolation valves located at the nearest valve stations (stations 14-a and 14-b). a temporary blind was installed at the damage site, and the leak was contained within 30 minutes. the incident was reported to the nrc (event #2026-01873) within the required 30-minute window, and a detailed investigation was launched to determine why the pipeline marker signs were not visible and why the contractor's one-call notification was not logged. the pipeline segment was taken out of service for repair and pressure testing before reinstatement.

NARRATIVE: on october 14, 2022 a 30-inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the riverbend processing plant experienced an unscheduled shutdown after a sudden pressure drop to 380 psig from its normal operating pressure of 720 psig. the line, installed in 1998, is equipped with a remotely operated mainline valve (mlv-3) that is normally held closed by a pneumatic actuator supplied from a 150-psi air reservoir. during the event, the control system logged an automatic open command to mlv-3 at 02:17, followed by a rapid depressurization and an estimated 4,200 mcf of natural gas released before the valve was manually closed at 02:45. investigation revealed that a recent software patch to the supervisory control and data acquisition (scada) system had inadvertently re-mapped the alarm clearance signal to the valve open command. the misconfiguration was not documented in the change control log, and the field technician who applied the patch was unaware of the valve's critical safety function. the primary cause was identified as an undocumented software change resulting in an inadvertent valve opening, with a contributing factor of inadequate change management procedures. the incident was reported to the appropriate regulatory agencies within the required one-hour window.

NARRATIVE: on april 12, 2023 a 24-inch carbon steel transmission line (line # 84) operating at 720 psig was being re-pressurized after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the segment runs through the foothills of the sierra and has a max allowable operating pressure (maop) of 850 psig. during the restart, the field supervisor instructed the crew to close the downstream isolation valves and increase the line pressure to 800 psig to meet downstream demand. however, the control room operator, unaware that a new high-pressure relief valve had been installed at the mountain ridge station with a set pressure of 770 psig, approved the increase. the line pressure continued to rise and at 2:45 pm the relief valve opened, venting approximately 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere for about ten minutes before the control system automatically reduced pressure. the release triggered a reportable event to the state and phmsa. investigation found the root cause to be a failure to update the pressure operating limits in the central control database after the valve replacement and a miscommunication between field operations and gas control that led to an unauthorized pressure increase beyond the relief setting.

NARRATIVE: (on april 12, 2025, a maintenance crew performed a planned pigging operation on section 14 of line # 472, a 10" stainless steel transmission conduit with a 530# maop, operating at 470# during normal service). the line had been scheduled for a pig pass to clear accumulated debris that had been identified during a routine inspection on march 28, 2025. at 02:15 am local time, the crew positioned the pigging head at the upstream valve station and closed all downstream isolation valves. a field engineer, jr. m. harris, was assigned to monitor the pressure transducer while the pigging crew, led by contractor l. t. singh, performed the purge sequence. however, due to a misread of the operating manual, the engineer mistakenly set the upstream pressure limit to 520# instead of the required 480#, believing the line was still at a reduced operating pressure. once the pig passed and the purge valve was opened at 02:45 am, the upstream pressure spiked to 525#, exceeding the set limit of the upstream relief valve calibrated at 520#. the relief valve opened to atmosphere at 02:47 am, releasing approximately 8.2 mmcf of natural gas. the incident was reported to phmsa within 24 hours, and the operator conducted a root-cause analysis that identified the incorrect pressure setting as the primary operational error.

NARRATIVE: on march 15, 2024 at 09:42 am (est), compressor station 312 in virginia experienced an unscheduled shutdown (uss) after a 10-inch carbon steel line (bwp 1400 psi) began to vent through a partially open cross-over valve (cv-312). the valve was located in the high-pressure section of the main transmission line and was operated manually by a field crew using a handheld remote. during the routine pressure-drop test, the crew opened the valve to 10% of its travel to check for leaks, but the operator did not verify the valve position with the station's hmi or the position sensor. the valve remained in an open state when the compressor was brought online, causing a rapid pressure decline to 650 psi. as the line pressure dropped, the downstream relief valve (rv-312) operated at 650 psi setpoint and opened, discharging 4,200 mcf of gas to the atmosphere. the event caused a 120-minute outage of the compressor. post-incident investigation found that the operator had used a portable battery-powered test lead to energize the valve actuator instead of the scheduled hmi control sequence. the valve actuator was also missing a calibrated limit switch, which prevented the system from automatically shutting the valve when the compressor returned to normal pressure. corrective actions include retraining of crew on valve-operation protocols, installation of a redundant position indicator, and revision of the daily pressure-drop test procedure to require hmi verification before any manual valve operation.

NARRATIVE: on august 5 2024 at 14:32 (pst), the eastern interconnect line 42kpsi, 24-inch schedule 80 steel, experienced a rapid depressurization event following an incorrect manual override of the automatic pressure relief valve (aprv). the operator mistakenly set the aprv setpoint to 45 psi instead of the required 15 psi while attempting a routine pressure test. within 12 seconds the line pressure surged to 48 psi, causing the downstream flare stack valve to trip and the line to vent 2.3 mcf of natural gas into the atmosphere. emergency responders were dispatched to the site; two employees sustained minor skin burns from the hot gas and were treated at the local clinic. the incident prompted an immediate shutdown of all downstream pumps and a full inspection of the aprv system. the root cause analysis identified a training gap and a missing lockout tag during the pressure test. corrective actions include updated operating procedures, mandatory lockout/tagout, and a refresher training program for all field operators.

NARRATIVE: on 7-12-2025, a contractor was performing a line-to-line pigging operation on a 36-inch, 4-mm-thick stainless steel pipeline running 150 miles between the north distribution hub and the east storage complex. the pipeline was rated for 7500 psi and operating at 6800 psi during the scheduled work. the contractor's pigger crew had received a brief refresher on the pigging procedure but had not reviewed the latest operating manual update that reduced the allowable pigging pressure to 6000 psi after the installation of a new high-temperature pigging valve. the crew selected the wrong pigging fluid and set the back-pressure gauge to 7200 psi, believing it to be within safe limits. as the pig entered the pipe, the pressure sensor read 7200 psi, and the pigger operator, noticing the reading, increased the back-pressure by adding more fluid until the pressure reached 7900 psi. the pipe's pressure-relief valve, calibrated for 7500 psi, was tripped, venting the line and causing a sudden pressure drop that triggered a rapid depressurization shock wave. the shock wave cracked a 4-mm weld seam near the pigging valve, producing a small gas release that ignited in the presence of residual hydrocarbons. the contractor's incorrect pressure operation was determined to be the primary cause of the incident, and the company has revised the pigging procedures to require pre-job confirmation of pressure limits and re-training of all pigging personnel.

NARRATIVE: on march 12, 2025, at approximately 9:45 a.m., the east valley compressor station's 24-inch carbon steel transmission line experienced an abrupt rupture during a routine pressure test. the test crew had incorrectly set the test pressure to 1,800 psi, exceeding the line's design pressure of 1,200 psi by 600 psi. the line had been previously corroded, with a wall thickness reduction of 15% at the test section, calculated to be 0.25 inches from the nominal 0.5 inches. when the line was pressurized to 1,800 psi, the material failed, releasing roughly 4,500 mcf of natural gas. the rupture created a flash fire, igniting a nearby flare stack and causing two injuries with minor burns. the station was immediately shut down and the surrounding area evacuated. an internal investigation determined that the pressure setpoint was incorrectly entered into the pressure control system, and that the operator failed to confirm the actual gauge reading before energizing the line. corrective actions included implementing a double-check procedure for pressure tests, retraining all operators on pressure-rating limits, and installing a redundant pressure interlock on the test valve. the station was back in service on april 15, 2025 after a full integrity inspection and replacement of the corroded line segment.

NARRATIVE: on august 14, 2025 at 06:42 (cst), the westfield compression station on the 24-inch carbon steel main (api 5l x65) experienced an unintended pressure surge. the station control engineer initiated a manual start-up of the downstream booster compressor while the upstream inlet valve was still partially open from a previous maintenance cycle. the inlet pressure was 820 psig, and the booster was set to increase downstream pressure to 1050 psig. because the inlet valve had not been fully closed, the sudden addition of compressor flow caused a rapid pressure rise to 1320 psig, exceeding the design limit of the 24-inch pipe segment. a section of the pipe near the valve manifold, which had a previously repaired girth weld, ruptured, releasing approximately 12,400 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetlands. emergency shutdown was manually triggered at 06:48, and the area was isolated. no injuries were reported, but local wildlife was impacted. the incident investigation concluded that the engineer failed to verify valve position before compressor start-up, and that the station's standard operating procedure for sequential valve closure was not followed. corrective actions include revising the start-up checklist, implementing an interlock to prevent compressor activation with inlet valve partially open, and retraining all operators on valve sequencing.

NARRATIVE: on october 14, 2024 at 09:45 mst, the south ridge compression unit 12 experienced an unscheduled vent. the unit was being brought back online after a maintenance shutdown when the operator manually opened the suction isolation valve using a handheld key switch instead of the hmi command. the valve was intended to remain closed until the downstream pressure reached 550 psig, but the manual actuation allowed gas at 720 psig to flow into the 20-inch carbon steel suction line. a downstream pressure transducer was out of calibration, reading 480 psig, so the automatic shutdown logic never engaged. the vent valve opened when the unit pressure exceeded its high-pressure alarm setpoint of 800 psig, releasing approximately 12,416 mcf of natural gas to the atmosphere over 18 minutes. investigation revealed that the portable key switch had been left energized from a previous test and that the operator was not aware of the pending high-pressure condition because the scada display was offline for a software upgrade. corrective actions include reinstating lockout-tagout procedures for handheld switches, recalibrating all pressure transmitters, and updating the start-up checklist to require verification of the scada communication status before valve actuation.

NARRATIVE: on 3/14/2023 at 07:42 am cdt, western interregional pipelines (wip) received an alarm from the control room indicating an unexpected pressure rise in the 24-inch mainline feeding the desert ridge compression hub, located in el paso county, texas. the line, a 2-1/2 in api 5l x70 carbon steel pipe, was scheduled for a routine start-up after a 48-hour maintenance shutdown. during the start-up, the field operator manually opened the upstream isolation valve (valve-b13) to 75 % instead of the prescribed 25 % open position, causing a rapid influx of gas from the upstream storage cavern at approximately 1150 psig. the sudden surge exceeded the design set-point of 1000 psig and triggered the downstream safety relief valve (sr-v07). the relief valve lifted, but due to an improperly seated o-ring, it failed to reseat, allowing a continuous release of gas through the vent stack. emergency services were dispatched at 07:55 am cdt and arrived on site at 08:12 am cdt. the release was isolated by closing the downstream isolation valve (valve-c21) at 08:20 am cdt. a total of 3500 scf of natural gas was vented before the situation was stabilized. the incident was reported to the nrc at 09:05 am cdt. subsequent investigation identified the incorrect manual valve opening as the primary operational error; wip revised the start-up procedure and added interlock verification to prevent manual override beyond 30 % opening.

NARRATIVE: on july 14, 2022, at 03:12 am, midwest pipeline corporation (mpc) received an automatic shutdown alarm from its 20-inch carbon steel transmission line (schedule 80, s355) at the riverbend compression station, nebraska. the line was being pressure-tested at 1,150 psi after a recent weld repair on a 30-ft segment. a technician used the handheld esd controller to isolate the test section, but inadvertently pressed the "open bypass" key instead of "close bypass." this action opened valve rb-12a, a 4-inch bypass valve that diverts flow to the downstream relief manifold. the bypass opened while the test pump continued to increase pressure, causing an uncontrolled surge that exceeded the pipe's design limit of 1,200 psi. within seconds the pipe's longitudinal seam cracked near the weld, releasing approximately 8 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding yard. the emergency shutdown system engaged at 03:16 am, limiting the release. investigation revealed that the handheld controller's key layout was not intuitive and the operator had not been retrained on the updated bypass procedure after the recent software upgrade. mpc has since revised the controller interface, instituted mandatory quarterly refresher training for all esd operators, and installed a physical key interlock on bypass valves to prevent accidental activation during pressure testing.

NARRATIVE: a 30-inch carbon steel transmission line operating at 820 psi was scheduled for a routine restart after a planned shutdown at the marisol gas gathering station. the line had been isolated with a 24-inch block valve and a 4-inch bypass valve was left open for pigging. during the restart, the station operator manually opened the bypass valve to re-pressurize the line but failed to verify that the block valve had been fully closed. as the 1500 hp centrifugal compressors came online, pressure built up rapidly behind the partially closed block valve, creating a pressure surge of approximately 1500 psi at the upstream end. the surge exceeded the design rating of a recently welded girth joint near milepost 27.5, causing the weld to fail and a 6-inch rupture to open. natural gas escaped, forming a vapor cloud that ignited when a nearby hot-work torch was used for a maintenance cut. the flash fire burned a crew of three, causing second-degree burns to two workers. investigation revealed the operator had not followed the standard operating procedure for valve sequencing and had not performed the required pressure check with the handheld gauge before initiating compressor start-up. corrective actions included revising the valve-lockout checklist, retraining all operators on sequential valve operations, and installing an automated interlock to prevent compressor start when the block valve is not fully closed.

NARRATIVE: on 09/14/2025 at 22:07, the crew performing routine pigging on the 30-inch carbon steel transmission line (rated 1200 psi) at the riverbend compression station opened the bypass valve without confirming that the line isolation clamps were fully engaged. the isolation clamps had been manually tightened earlier in the shift, but the lockout tag was never placed. after the bypass valve was opened, gas from the 1150 psi mainline entered the pigging loop, raising the pressure in the 24-inch pig trap to approximately 950 psi, well above its design limit of 750 psi. within three minutes the pig trap's relief valve lifted, releasing a high-velocity jet of natural gas into the adjacent yard. the release ignited when a nearby welding torch, being used for a scheduled flange repair, struck an exposed gas plume, producing a flash fire that damaged the torch stand and caused minor burns to two technicians. post-incident review showed the operator had relied on a handheld pressure gauge that was still calibrated for the low-pressure pigging circuit and failed to verify the mainline pressure before opening the bypass. corrective actions included revising the pigging standard operating procedure to require dual-point pressure verification and retraining all field personnel on lockout-tagout compliance.

NARRATIVE: on july 14, 2024 at 06:42 am, the western ridge compression station reported an unexpected pressure rise in line 24, a 20-inches carbon steel main feeding the northfield gathering system. the control room had just completed a scheduled startup of compressor c-3 after a three-month maintenance outage. an operator manually opened the inlet isolation valve (13-inches) to restore feed gas while the automatic shutdown interlock on the suction-side pressure sensor was still active. the valve was left fully open for approximately 7 minutes, causing the suction pressure to climb to 1 800 psig, well above the design limit of 1 200 psig. the over-pressure triggered the high-pressure vent valve, releasing an estimated 12 mmscf of natural gas through the 6-inch vent stack before the emergency shutdown (esd) was initiated at 06:52 am. field crews arrived on site at 07:10 am, isolated the inlet valve and confirmed that the compressor surge valve had sealed. post-incident analysis indicated the operator had not verified the interlock status in the start-up checklist. corrective actions included revising the start-up procedure, adding a visual lock-out on the inlet isolation valve when the suction-side interlock is engaged, and conducting a refresher training on manual valve operations.

NARRATIVE: on april 7, 2023, maintenance crew at the midstream gathering station were executing a scheduled pigging operation on the 24" carbon steel transmission line that transports wet natural gas from the field hub to the processing plant. the line was isolated by closing the upstream isolation valve 12-45 (rated 1200 psig) and the downstream block valve 12-48. after confirming lockout/tagout, operators opened the pig trap vent valve to depressurize the segment. however, the crew mistakenly opened the pig trap vent valve with the pneumatic actuator set to "open-fast" instead of using the manual hand wheel, causing the valve to snap open beyond its design travel. this created an unintended large opening to the vent stack, which was equipped with a 90-degree elbow and a 10-inch flare tip intended for low-flow venting. simultaneously, a downstream pressure regulator failed to seal, allowing line pressure of approximately 950 psig to surge through the vent stack. the high-velocity gas struck the elbow, generating a force that fractured the vent stack flange and ejected the flare tip. approximately 18 mmcf of gas escaped before the emergency shutdown system isolated the line by automatically closing valve 12-45. the incident was attributed to the operator's incorrect use of the pneumatic actuator and failure to follow the standard manual venting procedure. subsequent corrective actions included retraining on valve actuation methods and reinstalling a reinforced vent stack with a pressure-rated design.

NARRATIVE: on october 3, 2024 at 14:27 the midland gas processing plant began a scheduled pigging operation on the 24-inch, 7-cr steel transmission line that carries sweet natural gas at a design pressure of 950 psig. the isolation procedure required the mainline isolation valve (mlv-12) to be closed and locked out before the pig launcher could be depressurized. the field crew, under time pressure, failed to verify that the lockout/tagout devices were fully engaged on mlv-12 and proceeded to open the vent valve to purge residual gas from the pig launcher. the vent valve was opened while the mainline remained pressurized, allowing gas at approximately 870 psig to flow through the 12-inch vent stack for roughly six minutes before the operator noticed the abnormal pressure drop on the control panel. a downstream pressure sensor recorded a rapid decrease from 945 psig to 420 psig, triggering the emergency shutdown system which automatically cycled the upstream shutdown valve. the incident resulted in an unplanned release of an estimated 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere and a brief plant shutdown. the subsequent investigation cited failure to follow the lockout/tagout protocol and premature venting as the primary operational errors. corrective actions include a mandatory lockout/tagout verification checklist and additional hands-on training for all pigging crews.

NARRATIVE: on september 5, 2023 at approximately 04:27 am cdt the midwest 30-inch carbon steel transmission line (mr 84231) experienced an unexpected emergency shutdown (esd) while the line was being cycled from idle to full load. the line normally operates at a maximum allowable operating pressure (maop) of 850 psi, with a design limit of 1150 psi. during the start-up sequence, the operator manually opened the upstream 30-inch block valve (bv-12) and the downstream 36-inch control valve (cv-7) without confirming the position of the auxiliary gas-supply valve (agv-3). agv-3 had been left in the open position from a prior maintenance activity intended to purge the line, allowing additional supply gas to enter the system. as a result, line pressure rose to 940 psi, exceeding the maop by 10 %. the high-pressure alarm triggered the esd system, closing the 30-inch emergency shutdown valve (esd-30) and venting gas to the nearby relief vent. subsequent investigation showed no equipment failure; the fire detector and pressure transmitters functioned correctly. the root cause was determined to be the failure to reset agv-3 to the closed position after maintenance, a procedural oversight that will be addressed with revised lock-out/tag-out procedures and additional operator training.

NARRATIVE: on april 3, 2022, the hillcrest gathering system experienced an unplanned release of natural gas from a 24-inch carbon steel main that transports gas from the riverbend field to the processing plant. the main is normally operated at 1,200 psig and is equipped with a series-rated valve at milepost 12.5 that is controlled by the central control room via scada. during a scheduled pressure reduction to 950 psig, the control operator entered the wrong setpoint for the valve actuator and inadvertently commanded a slow open instead of a close. the valve remained partially open for approximately 45 minutes, allowing gas to escape through a 0.5-inch leak that had developed at a previous repair weld that was not fully re-qualified. field personnel first noticed a faint odor at the south-east perimeter of the valve house at 14:22 local time and reported it to the control room. the control room operator, believing the valve had been fully closed, did not dispatch a response team. by the time the leak was visually confirmed at 14:58, the pressure in the main had dropped to 820 psig and an estimated 2,800 mcf of gas had been released to the atmosphere. after the incident, the company revised the valve-actuation procedure to require a dual-confirmation step in scada and instituted a mandatory on-site visual verification for any pressure-setpoint changes exceeding 150 psig. additional training on setpoint entry and a lock-out verification for critical valves were also implemented.

NARRATIVE: during a scheduled integrity test on the 24-inch, 970 psi carbon steel transmission line (segment a-12) near the hillcrest regulator, the field crew was instructed to isolate the line by closing the upstream mainline isolation valve (mliv-01) and opening the downstream test bypass valve (tbv-07). the crew used a hand-held portable controller to energize the tbv-07 solenoid, believing the mliv-01 was fully seated. however, a recent maintenance log indicated that mliv-01 had been replaced with a new double-block-and-bleed valve but the position indicator on the hmi had not been calibrated. the crew did not verify the valve position on the control panel and instead relied on a visual check of the valve stem, which appeared closed but was actually 15 % open. when the test pressure was increased to 850 psi, gas began leaking from the junction between tbv-07 and the downstream pig launcher, creating a venting plume that triggered the emergency shutdown (esd) system. the esd valve failed to close because the power-gas supply to the esd network was offline for a scheduled upgrade, a condition not communicated to the crew. the leak persisted for 12 minutes before the manual shut-in was performed, releasing approximately 3,200 mcf of natural gas and causing a brief service interruption to two downstream customers. investigation highlighted the lack of verification of valve position on the hmi and the failure to coordinate the power-gas outage with field operations.

NARRATIVE: at approximately 02:45 am on september 14, 2025, a field operator at midwest transmission services (mts) initiated a restart of the mainline pump station 7b after a scheduled maintenance outage. the pump, a 1500 hp vertical turbine, was brought online without verifying that the downstream isolation valve 12-c had been fully closed. at 02:58 am the isolation valve was observed to be partially open, allowing gas to flow into the 24-inch carbon-steel mainline that was still depressurized from the outage. the sudden influx raised line pressure from 0 to 740 psig within seconds, exceeding the design limit of 720 psig. the over-pressurization caused a longitudinal crack to develop near the 5-mile marker, resulting in a release of approximately 850 mcf of natural gas that ignited after a nearby lightning strike. emergency response teams evacuated the area, sealed the leak with a quick-connect clamp, and vented the remaining gas. a post-incident investigation determined that the operator had skipped the required lock-out/tag-out verification step in the restart checklist and had not consulted the real-time pressure display before energizing the pump. mts revised its standard operating procedures to require a secondary electronic confirmation of valve position and added a mandatory pause of five minutes with pressure monitoring before any pump start-up. training modules were updated to emphasize lock-out/tag-out compliance for all pump station personnel.

NARRATIVE: on september 14, 2025, at approximately 08:46 mt, a rupture and subsequent fire occurred on the western interconnect 12 carbon-steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the river bend tie-in station, located about 3.2 mi southeast of blackrock, wy. the line had been isolated for a scheduled valve replacement on segment 4b, and after the work crew removed the old 24-in in-line isolation valve, the system was to be repressurized using the mainline packer. the operations technician manually opened the downstream block valve (bv-12) before the packer pressure had been equalized, resulting in a rapid pressure differential of roughly 950 psi (design pressure 800 psi, surge pressure 1200 psi) across the newly installed valve. the sudden surge caused a tensile overload at a previously repaired girth weld near milepost 12.4, leading to a circumferential rupture and immediate release of high-pressure natural gas. an ignition source from a nearby hot-work torch ignited the escaping mixture, producing a fireball that burned for approximately three minutes before emergency shutdown systems engaged. one crew member sustained second-degree burns and was transported to the regional medical center; the incident caused a temporary loss of service to 2,300 customers downstream. post-incident investigation cited the premature valve actuation and inadequate verification of pressure equalization as the primary operational errors.

NARRATIVE: pipeline segment 14, a 20" api 5l carbon steel pipe installed in 1992, rated for 900 psi, was operating at 720 psi when maintenance crews began a pressure reduction test on july 14, 2023. the procedure called for closing valve 14-22-a on the east side, then opening the downstream bleed valve 14-22-b to vent gas while the main line pressure was stepped down. the crew mistakenly opened valve 14-22-c, a 6" isolation valve on a parallel service line, instead of the intended 14-22-b. this caused a sudden pressure differential that forced gas from the main line into the service line, exceeding its 500-psi design limit. within seconds a loud pop was heard and a flash fire erupted at the valve rack, igniting a nearby fuel oil hose. two technicians received second-degree burns to their arms and a third-degree burn to one forearm; both were treated on-site and later transported to a regional burn center. the incident was reported to the operator and phmsa, and an investigation revealed that the valve tag plates were outdated and the crew relied on handwritten notes, leading to the incorrect valve operation. corrective actions included updating the valve identification system, retraining staff on isolation procedures, and revising the pressure reduction work plan.

NARRATIVE: on july 13, 2024 at approximately 14:20 local time, the control room at the riverbend gas processing facility observed a gradual rise in downstream pressure on the 30-inch carbon steel mainline feeding the eastbound distribution network. the scheduled increase in gas injection from the 24-inch upstream gathering line was initiated to meet a peak demand contract. the operations engineer entered a manual set point of 950 psig for the inlet regulator, exceeding the line's maximum allowable operating pressure of 900 psig. because the pressure relief valve at the downstream pigging station was still set to its default 880 psig opening pressure, the valve never opened. at 14:35 the supervisory control system generated a high-pressure alarm, but the engineer, assuming a sensor glitch, acknowledged the alarm and delayed corrective action. by 14:50 the pressure reached 1,018 psig, causing the low-temperature vent valve on the 30-inch line to lift, releasing an estimated 3,200 mcf of natural gas to atmosphere over the next 12 minutes. field crews arrived at 15:05, manually closed the vent valve, and initiated an emergency depressurization. post-incident analysis identified the incorrect manual set point entry and failure to verify relief valve settings as the primary contributors. corrective actions include revising the standard operating procedure for pressure set point changes and re-calibrating all downstream relief devices.

NARRATIVE: on august 14, 2022 at approximately 03:12 am local time, a maintenance crew was performing a pressure test on a 24-inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the northfield compression station. the line was rated for 1500 psig and contained dry natural gas at 1450 psig. the crew intended to isolate a 12-inch pig trap downstream by closing the pig-trap isolation valve (tag p-124) and then opening a bypass valve (tag b-87) to reroute flow through a temporary test loop. due to a mis-read of the valve position indicator, the operator opened the bypass valve while the pig-trap isolation valve remained partially open. this resulted in an uncontrolled surge of gas into the test loop, exceeding the design pressure of the temporary steel fittings (rated 1200 psig). a 4-inch relief valve on the loop lifted at 1300 psig, but the sudden release caused a high-velocity jet to escape from a loosened coupling, striking a technician standing on the platform. the technician sustained second-degree burns to the forearm and was evacuated to the nearest hospital. the incident was halted after the mainline was shut down and the bypass valve was closed. post-incident investigation revealed the error stemmed from an outdated valve-status board and lack of a lock-out/tag-out procedure for the isolation valve. the operator's workstation software has been updated to display real-time valve positions, a lock-out/tag-out protocol has been instituted for all isolation points, and the temporary test loop fittings have been replaced with components rated for the full line pressure. training sessions on valve-operation sequencing are being conducted for all field personnel.

NARRATIVE: on september 3, 2022 at 0837 local time, a utility technician from western pipelines was conducting a routine pressure test on a 20-inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x65) that transports natural gas at a design pressure of 900 psi near the hillcrest interchange. the test procedure called for increasing the downstream regulator set point from 650 psi to 720 psi while monitoring the isolation valve. the technician mistakenly entered the new set point on the upstream station controller instead of the downstream regulator, raising the upstream pressure to 820 psi. this caused the automatic shut-in valve to open partially, and the 12-inch bypass line, which was still connected to the high-pressure side, released gas into the surrounding easement. the vent persisted for approximately 12 minutes before the operator recognized the discrepancy, isolated the line, and closed the bypass. emergency services were notified at 0845, and a 3-person fire crew established a hot-work exclusion zone. no injuries or ignition occurred, but an estimated 18 mmcf of gas escaped, exceeding the dot reporting threshold. western pipelines filed a 24-hour report with the ferc, conducted a root-cause analysis, and instituted a dual-confirmation protocol for all set-point changes. corrective training for all field personnel was completed by october 15, 2022.

NARRATIVE: on july 14, 2022 at approximately 04:12 a.m., a routine maintenance crew arrived at the silver creek city gate station in columbia county, ne. the station feeds a 24-in. dsu carbon steel transmission line that normally operates at 560 psig delivering 22,000 dekatherms per hour. at 04:18 the crew began a scheduled isolation of the primary meter run to perform a pressure-drop test on the downstream regulator set. the technician manually closed the primary run valve (prv-03) and opened the bypass valve to maintain service. after completing the test at 04:33 the technician failed to close the bypass and, instead of re-opening prv-03, he mistakenly left the bypass fully open while simultaneously closing the auxiliary isolation valve that isolates the downstream line. this sequence caused the line to run unattended with the bypass in service, dropping the station outlet pressure to 210 psig, well below the under-pressure protection set point of 250 psig. the protection system automatically shut the downstream regulator, resulting in a loss of gas service to the city of silver creek. at 04:36 a high-low pressure alarm sounded; operators attempted to restore flow but could not re-open the primary valve because it remained locked in the closed position. the incident was reported internally at 05:10 and subsequently notified to the state pipeline safety commission and the national response center at 05:45. corrective actions include revising lockout/tagout procedures and implementing a dual-confirmation checklist for valve isolation steps.

NARRATIVE: on october 12, 2024, at approximately 06:42 am central time, a release event occurred on the western midland transmission system (wmts) while a routine line-swap was being performed on the 30-inch, carbon steel segment spanning the high plains interconnect. the work crew had been instructed to isolate valve b-2155 and open valve b-2158 to divert flow to the parallel 24-inch loop. due to an oversight, valve b-2155 remained fully open and valve b-2158 was only partially opened (30 %). as a result, the flow rate in the 30-inch line spiked to 2 500 mmcf/d, raising the pipeline inlet pressure from its normal 720 psig to 815 psig, exceeding the maop of 800 psig. at 06:48 am the high-pressure relief valve on the 30-inch suction header lifted (set point 800 psig), venting approximately 1 200 mcf of gas to the atmosphere over the next ten minutes. the downstream pressure reduction triggered a secondary relief valve on the 24-inch line (set point 650 psig) at 06:55 am, releasing an additional 850 mcf. emergency response was initiated at 07:03 am, and the control center isolated the affected segment by closing valve b-2162. investigations later determined the incident stemmed from the operator's failure to verify valve positions during the line-swap pre-job checklist and an ambiguous work instruction that did not require a second visual confirmation. corrective actions included revising the line-swap procedure to require dual-operator verification of all valve statuses, retraining crew members on the updated checklist, and installing a lock-out tag-out device on valve b-2155 during future swaps. the total gas loss was estimated at 2 050 mcf, surpassing the 3 000 mcf reporting threshold, and a phmsa 191.25(b) report was filed.

NARRATIVE: on september 14, 2023 at approximately 03:45 a.m. a field crew from western pipelines was performing a scheduled depressurization of a 24-inch, 75 psi carbon steel transmission line (segment id wp-12-b) to allow installation of a new pressure regulator station. the crew manually opened isolation valve iv-2143 upstream of the regulator without first confirming the downstream block valve bv-5678 was fully closed. the block valve had been left in a partially open position from a previous maintenance activity, resulting in residual pressure of 42 psi remaining in the line. when the crew released the isolation valve, gas escaped through a vent line that was only rated for 10 psi, creating a vapor cloud that ignited when a nearby hot-work torch was used for pipe coating preparation. the incident caused a flash fire, minor injuries to two crew members, and a temporary loss of service for 3 hours. investigation determined the root cause was a failure to follow the standard operating procedure for sequential valve isolation and to verify valve positions via the control system read-back. corrective actions included revising the depressurization checklist, adding a mandatory electronic lockout confirmation for block valves, and conducting a refresher training on valve sequencing for all operations personnel.

NARRATIVE: on august 14, 2025, at approximately 07:45 cdt, the west ridge compressor station was undergoing a routine start-up after a planned maintenance outage. the station operator manually opened the low-pressure suction governor valve (lp-gv-214) to initiate the compressor start-up sequence, but inadvertently bypassed the interlock that requires the downstream suction pressure transmitter (pt-305) to be in the ready state. as a result, the compressor reached a surge pressure of 1,250 psig, exceeding the design limit of 1,150 psig for the 30-inch carbon steel suction line. the surge caused the suction line's pressure relief valve (prv-07) to lift, releasing approximately 4.2 mmcf of natural gas to the atmosphere through the vent stack. the operator noticed the high-pressure alarm, shut down the compressor, and isolated the suction line. emergency response was dispatched at 08:12 cdt and arrived on site at 08:46 cdt. an investigation later revealed that the operator had not updated the start-up procedure after a recent modification to the pressure control logic, which now required a digital lockout that was still active. corrective actions included revising the standard operating procedure, retraining all start-up personnel on the new lockout requirements, and implementing a software check that prevents manual valve opening when the interlock is engaged.

NARRATIVE: on august 3, 2022, the riverbend gathering system experienced an unintended release of natural gas at the hillcrest pump station. the 24-inch carbon steel mainline, rated for 1100 psig, was being operated at a scheduled pressure of 950 psig when the upstream booster compressor was manually set to 1150 psig to compensate for a downstream flow restriction. the field operator failed to update the pump control panel and inadvertently opened the 18-inch isolation valve downstream of the pressure regulator, allowing the over-pressurized gas to bypass the regulator and enter the low-pressure distribution network. the gas escaped through a 4-inch relief vent stack for approximately 92 minutes before the alarm was acknowledged at 14:07 local time. during the incident, the scada system had generated a warning tag to alert operators to verify valve position after any manual pressure change, but the tag had been cleared during a recent software patch without proper documentation. after the release, the operator manually closed the isolation valve at 15:39 and the system was depressurized to 800 psig. subsequent investigation identified the lack of a lock-out procedure for manual pressure adjustments and the removal of the scada warning tag as root causes. corrective actions included reinstating the warning tag, implementing a mandatory lock-out/tag-out protocol for manual pressure changes, and revising the operator training program to emphasize verification of valve positions after any manual override.

NARRATIVE: on 06/12/2024 at 07:45 a.m., the 24-inch mainline feeding the east field was scheduled for a routine pressure increase to accommodate higher demand. the control operator mistakenly entered 1,600 psi as the target set point instead of the approved 1,200 psi. the automated pressure regulator responded by opening the upstream booster pump, and the line pressure climbed to 1,640 psi within eight minutes, exceeding the design limit of 1,550 psi for the carbon-steel pipe. pressure relief valves on the downstream metering station opened at 1,600 psi, venting natural gas into the surrounding low-lying area. field personnel observed a hissing sound and reported a gas plume to the control center. the incident command team was alerted, and an emergency shut-in was initiated; the downstream block valve was closed manually while the upstream booster pump was tripped. the gas release was contained within 12 minutes, but a section of the 24-inch pipe showed signs of strain and a small leak was detected at a girth weld 0.3 mile downstream of the metering station. the line was isolated, depressurized, and the compromised pipe segment was replaced. the root cause was identified as an incorrect set-point entry by the operator, and a software lockout was added to prevent future manual overrides beyond the 1,250 psi limit.

NARRATIVE: on march 3, 2022, a maintenance crew was performing a pressure reduction on a 24-inch api 5l x65 carbon steel transmission line near the edwards county pump station. the line was operating at 850 psig and was to be isolated for valve replacement on the mainline. at 08:15, technicians opened the upstream isolation valve and began venting to atmosphere using a 2-inch vent stack rated for 500 psig. the vent stack was installed without a required pressure-relief snubbing device, and the crew failed to verify the vent stack's rating against the line pressure. as the pressure dropped, a sudden "pop" was heard and a jet of natural gas erupted from the vent stack, projecting approximately 30 feet downwind. operators on the control room observed a rapid pressure drop to 120 psig on scada, but did not immediately initiate an emergency shut-in. the gas plume triggered an automatic isolation of the downstream segment at 08:22, and the area was evacuated. two crew members suffered minor injuries from the blast; both were treated on site and released. investigation later determined that the vent stack installation procedure was not followed, the incorrect venting equipment was used, and the required pressure-relief device was omitted, leading to the uncontrolled release. the line was fully depressurized and repaired, and service was restored on march 5, 2022.

NARRATIVE: at the ridgecrest compression station, operators were preparing for a scheduled hydrostatic test on the 30-inch mainline (api 5l x80 carbon steel, operating at 1150 psi). the procedure required isolation of the downstream block valve (valve b-45-02) and opening of the test isolation valve (valve t-45-07). due to a misinterpretation of the work order, the control console was used to open valve t-45-07 before valve b-45-02 was fully closed. the downstream block valve remained partially seated, allowing gas from the 24-inch feeder (operating at 1050 psi) to flow into the test section. as the test pump began pressurizing the isolated segment, the unintended flow caused the relief valve on the test manifold (relief-t-45-03, set at 1300 psi) to lift. approximately 4 500 mcf of natural gas escaped through the vent stack before the operator realized the error and manually closed the relief valve at 02:17 a.m. the incident triggered an emergency shutdown, the test was aborted, and the vented volume was reported to the regulatory authority. corrective actions included revising the isolation checklist, adding interlock logic to prevent opening of test valves until block valves confirm closed status, and retraining personnel on procedural sequencing.

NARRATIVE: on 09/14/2023 at 07:22 am, the field operator at the riverbend compression station initiated a manual start-up of the 24-inch mainline suction pump without verifying the upstream isolation valve position. the isolation valve on the southbound feeder line was inadvertently left open, allowing product from the adjacent 20-inch gathering line to flow into the suction inlet at an unexpected temperature of 140 degrees f. the pump, rated for 120 degrees f inlet, experienced a rapid rise in bearing temperature and tripped its high-temperature shutdown at 07:35 am. meanwhile, the downstream pressure transducer on the 24-inch discharge header read 1150 psig, exceeding the design limit of 1050 psig, and the automatic relief valve at the downstream metering station began to lift at 07:38 am. the operator, focused on the pump alarm, failed to notice the rising pressure on the control screen and did not close the feeder isolation valve until 07:50 am after a secondary alarm sounded. the delayed isolation caused a brief over-pressurization event that resulted in a small vent to the atmosphere at the metering station, releasing approximately 15 scf of natural gas. the incident was logged in part e5.f and a corrective action was issued to require a double-check verification of isolation valve status before any manual pump start-up.

NARRATIVE: on june 14, 2025 at 08:42 a.m. central standard time, the midwest north gas transmission facility experienced an unplanned release of natural gas near the hickory ridge metering station. the facility consists of a 30-inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line rated for 720 psi operating pressure, feeding a downstream 24-inch line through a dual-block valve assembly. during a scheduled pressure test, the field operator opened the upstream isolation valve (valve-a) to isolate a 3-mile section for inspection, but mistakenly left the downstream block valve (valve-b) closed. after the test, the operator re-pressurized the upstream line to 650 psi without first opening valve-b, causing pressure to build in the isolated segment. the built-up pressure exceeded the design limit of the temporary pig-in-place barrier (rated 600 psi) and forced the barrier open, ejecting a 2-foot section of 6-inch pigging pipe into the surrounding right-of-way. the release was detected by the scada alarm from a sudden drop in downstream flow and a rise in acoustic emission sensors. emergency shutdown procedures were initiated within 25 seconds, and the line was isolated with the emergency shut-off valve. there were no injuries, but the incident resulted in a loss of product estimated at 4.2 mmcf and required repair of the pig-in-place barrier and replacement of the ejected pipe segment. the operator's procedural checklist was revised to require verification of downstream valve status before re-pressurization.

NARRATIVE: at 07:42 am mst on october 3, 2022 the austin-hutto pipeline mainline (24-in. carbon steel, design pressure 1500 psi, operating at 820 psi) was scheduled for a pigging run to remove accumulated paraffin. the pig launcher was manually set to a low-pressure purge of 150 psi, but the field operator mistakenly keyed the pig-in-line valve to the high-pressure service position (800 psi) while the purge was still active. as the pig entered the high-pressure segment, the sudden pressure jump caused a rapid increase in line pressure to 1050 psi, exceeding the rated limit of the downstream pressure regulator (rated to 950 psi). the regulator failed to close, and the over-pressurized gas opened a relief valve on the 12-in. downstream branch, venting natural gas to the atmosphere for approximately 6 minutes before the operator recognized the abnormal pressure reading on the scada display. the venting released an estimated 3.2 mmcf of gas, which was reported to the nrc at 10:15 am mst the same day. corrective actions included retraining all personnel on pig-launch procedures, installing a lock-out interlock that prevents high-service valve actuation during purge, and conducting a pressure-test of all downstream regulators. a supplemental report was filed on october 7 to amend the initial incident description and to document the lock-out implementation.

NARRATIVE: on friday, september 14, 2022, at approximately 0830 hours, the field crew of western midstream began a scheduled maintenance shutdown on a 24-inch api 5l x70 carbon steel transmission line (maop 800 psi) that was operating at 560 psi transporting dry natural gas from the hillcrest gathering system to the southfield processing facility. the work plan called for a full isolation of the 3-mile segment between milepost 12.4 and 15.7, followed by a hot-tapping operation to install a new pressure-taker valve. the crew mistakenly opened the downstream isolation valve before confirming that the upstream valve had been fully closed and that the line was depressurized. as a result, a sudden surge of gas at 520 psi escaped through a partially opened vent valve that had been left connected to a temporary pig launcher. the gas accumulated in a low-lying trench where a diesel generator was being pre-heated. an ignition source from the generator's exhaust ignited the gas cloud, producing a flash fire that burned three workers; two suffered second-degree burns to their arms and were transported to the regional burn center, while the third sustained a first-degree burn to the face. the fire was extinguished by onsite emergency response within ten minutes. the incident was reported to the phmsa, the nrc (incident # 2022-0187), and the state oil and gas commission. the line was purged, inspected, and returned to service on september 18 after replacement of the vent valve and a revised lock-out/tag-out procedure was implemented.

NARRATIVE: on april 12, 2025, at approximately 07:46 a.m., a crew was performing a hot-tap on the 24-inch, carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) at the ridgeview junction in west texas. the line was scheduled to be isolated at 1500 psi and purged with nitrogen to a residual pressure of less than 5 psi before the tap. the isolation valve on the upstream side was manually turned half-closed by the rig operator, believing the automatic valve had already sealed the line. after confirming nitrogen flow, the operator engaged the tapping hammer and began drilling into the pipe wall. within seconds, a sudden surge of natural gas escaped from the incomplete seal, forcing the nitrogen purge to reverse direction. the escaping gas ignited when the spark generated by the hammer struck a metal fragment, producing a flash fire that singed the operator's jacket and caused minor burns to a nearby technician. post-incident analysis revealed that the operator had incorrectly assumed the automated isolation sequence had completed, failed to verify full closure with the pressure gauge, and did not follow the required lock-out/tag-out procedure. corrective actions included retraining on valve position verification, reinforcement of lock-out/tag-out compliance, and installation of a secondary visual indicator for isolation status.

NARRATIVE: on april 7, 2022 a scheduled integrity check was performed on the east valley 30-inch carbon steel transmission line (api 5l x70) near the meadow ridge pump station. the line was operating at 950 psig with a flow of 4200 mmscfd. at 08:14 the control system set point for rov-7423 was changed from 100% open to 0% to initiate a full-closure test. the operator omitted the required 12-minute flow-reduction step, leaving the line at full throughput while the valve began to travel. at 08:18 the valve was 45% closed when a high-pressure alarm triggered at 1020 psig, exceeding the maop of 1000 psig. the downstream pressure transducer, which had been calibrated six months prior, reported a false low reading, causing the control algorithm to command additional closure. by 08:20 the valve was stuck at 70% open and the upstream pressure spiked to 1085 psig, breaching the over-pressure protection set point of 1050 psig. an automatic shut-down valve downstream failed to open due to a missed maintenance check, resulting in a release of approximately 1800 scf of natural gas through a ruptured flange at the 30-inch segment. emergency response was activated at 08:23, and the incident was reported to the state commission at 09:05. the post-incident review identified the operator's deviation from the standard operating procedure and the lack of a real-time pressure verification step as root causes.

NARRATIVE: on july 7, 2023, at approximately 1515 hours, a crew from western pipeline services was conducting a scheduled tie-in of a new 12-inch carbon steel transmission line to the existing 24-inch mainline at the pine ridge junction, located near milepost 112.5 in central texas. the tie-in required the temporary isolation of the mainline using a double block and bleed (dbb) arrangement. the field supervisor instructed the operators to close the upstream block valve (valve a-12) and depressurize the section before removing the downstream block valve (valve b-12). however, the operator mistakenly opened valve a-12 instead of closing it, while valve b-12 remained fully open. as a result, the mainline pressure of 850 psig was allowed to flow directly into the isolated segment, causing a rapid pressure surge. within seconds, a 1-inch relief vent on the tie-in manifold lifted, releasing a visible plume of natural gas. the crew activated the emergency shutdown (esd) at 1520 hours, but the delayed recognition of the valve mis-positioning caused a 4-minute exposure. the incident was reported to the state oil and gas commission at 1545 hours and to the pipeline safety authority at 1550 hours. the post-incident review identified incorrect valve operation and lack of a verification checklist as the primary root cause.

NARRATIVE: on june 14, 2025 at 07:23 am cdt, a maintenance crew arrived at the river bend compression station to perform a scheduled vent and bleed of the 24-inch carbon steel mainline after a pigging run. the crew was instructed to close the upstream isolation valve (tag b-101) and open the downstream vent valve (tag v-202) to release residual pressure before removing the pig launcher. the technician mistakenly opened the isolation valve instead of the vent valve, allowing line pressure of approximately 1 450 psi to flow directly into the vent stack. the sudden pressure surge forced the vent stack's 2-inch stainless steel relief pipe to rupture, releasing high-pressure natural gas into the surrounding yard. emergency shutdown was initiated by the control room within 45 seconds, and the automatic block valve downstream (tag b-303) closed, isolating the segment. the rupture was patched and the vent stack replaced. two crew members sustained minor injuries from the blast wave and were treated on site. investigation revealed the valve tag numbers were reversed on the field panel, leading to the operator's error. corrective actions include relabeling all valve panels, revising the standard operating procedure to require a double-check verification, and conducting a refresher training on valve identification for all field personnel.

NARRATIVE: at 07:45 am on 15 august 2024, the western interregional gas transmission system control center received a low-pressure alarm on line w-212, a 30-in. api-5l x80 carbon steel pipeline operating at 850 psig. the alarm triggered an automatic shutdown of the upstream regulator station r-47. an on-site operator proceeded to isolate the line for maintenance, but inadvertently opened valve v-3212, a 24-in. isolation valve on the downstream side, while the regulator remained in a closed "maintenance" position. this created a pressure differential that forced gas to bypass the regulator and flow through an unused bypass loop that had not been purged. the gas entered a 12-in. vent line terminating at a temporary vent stack that had been removed for welding work two days earlier. as a result, high-energy natural gas escaped to the atmosphere at an estimated rate of 2,400 mcf/d. the released gas accumulated in a low-lying ditch, ignited by a static discharge from a nearby diesel-powered pump, causing a flash fire that burned three crew members, one of whom required hospitalization. after the event, investigators determined that the operator had not consulted the revised bypass-operation procedure and had failed to verify the valve position against the electronic log. corrective actions included retraining on bypass protocols, updating the standard operating procedure, and implementing a dual-approval step for any valve changes during maintenance.

NARRATIVE: on may 5, 2022 the operators at gathering station r-12 were completing a routine pigging operation on the 30-inch mainline that carries raw natural gas from the shale field to the processing plant. after the pig passed, the crew began repressurizing the line using the 10-inch loading arm attached to the south side gate valve. the supervisor instructed technician j. williams to close the isolation valve on the north side before opening the loading arm, but he mistakenly thought the valve was already closed and opened the loading arm while the north isolation valve remained open. the line pressure rose quickly to 740 psig, exceeding the design limit of 700 psig for the downstream segment. within minutes a gash appeared at a previously repaired weld on a 24-inch carbon steel pipe near milepost 12.3, releasing an estimated 5.2 mmscf of gas into the surrounding wetlands. emergency shutdown (esd) was initiated by the control room after the pressure alarm tripped, and the line was isolated by closing the mainline valve and the emergency vent. response crews evacuated the area, installed a temporary blind flange, and later replaced the damaged pipe section and re-torqued all adjacent flange bolts to meet api 6d specifications. a post-incident review cited the failure to verify valve position as the primary operational error.

NARRATIVE: on august 14, 2021 at approximately 07:18 am, a routine restart of the 24-inch high-pressure natural gas transmission line on the riverbend compression station, located near springfield, il, resulted in an unplanned release of gas. the line, rated for 1,200 psi and operating at 950 psi, was being brought back online after a scheduled maintenance shutdown. the field operator opened the mainline isolation valve (tag b-12) before confirming that the downstream 30-inch shut-off valve (tag c-07) was fully seated. a pressure differential of 300 psi caused the downstream valve to fail to close completely, allowing gas to vent through a vent stack designed for low-flow relief. within seconds, a jet of gas ignited when it contacted a nearby hot-work torch used for a separate welding task, producing a flash fire that burned the operator's forearm and singed a nearby control panel. emergency shutdown was initiated at 07:22 am, and the fire was extinguished by 07:26 am. the incident investigation determined that the operator's sequence of valve operations was contrary to the approved start-up procedure; no equipment malfunction was identified. the company has since revised the start-up checklist and provided additional hands-on training for all station personnel.

NARRATIVE: after routine pressure testing of the 24-inch, schedule 40 carbon steel main at the midstream processing facility, the operator received a scada alarm indicating a pressure drop from the set point of 950 psi to 820 psi. believing the drop was due to a transient pump start-up, the technician manually opened the bypass valve (bv-12) without confirming that the primary pump had reached full speed. the bypass valve was left fully open for approximately five minutes while the primary pump was still throttling down. during this interval the downstream line pressure spiked to 1 120 psi, exceeding the design limit of 1 000 psi. the excessive pressure caused a girth weld failure at the 3-mile marker, resulting in a 6-inch rupture that released approximately 340 mmcf of natural gas into the surrounding low-lying terrain. after the incident, investigators found that the operator had not followed the standard operating procedure requiring verification of pump speed and pressure stabilization before bypass actuation. the bypass valve was also found to be incorrectly labeled, contributing to the mis-operation. corrective actions included re-training staff on pump-bypass sequencing, updating valve identification signage, and installing an interlock to prevent manual bypass opening until pump speed is confirmed.

NARRATIVE: on august 9, 2024 a field operator at the midland east gas compression station began a scheduled restart of compressor c-3 after a routine maintenance shutdown. the unit, a 4-stage centrifugal compressor rated for 1200 psi inlet pressure, was tied to a 30-inch api 5l carbon steel transmission line carrying dry natural gas at a nominal flow of 7500 mmscfd. the standard restart procedure required the inlet pressure regulator to be set at 950 psi before the compressor could be brought online. the operator mistakenly set the regulator to 1150 psi, a value reserved for peak summer demand, and failed to verify the setpoint on the handheld digital gauge. within three minutes of startup the compressor surged, increasing line pressure to 1380 psi, exceeding the line's maximum allowable operating pressure of 1300 psi. the over-pressurization triggered the high-pressure safety valve at milepost 12.4, which released approximately 450 mcf of gas to the atmosphere before the valve reseated. alarms sounded, the operator shut down c-3, and the control room isolated the affected segment. post-incident review identified the incorrect regulator setpoint and lack of a dual-verification step as the root causes, leading to an update of the restart checklist and additional training for all station personnel.

NARRATIVE: on 5 october 2023 at approximately 04:23 utc a maintenance crew was performing a routine pigging operation on the north ridge transmission line (segment b-12, 24-inch carbon steel, design pressure 1 200 psig) near the hillcrest compression station. the crew isolated the line at valve a-34 and b-56, but failed to verify the lock-out of the downstream control valve c-9 after completing the pig run. at 04:38 the control system automatically opened valve c-9 to restart flow, unaware that the line remained partially depressurized from the pigging. gas velocity surged to 3 500 ft/s, exceeding the safe operating limit, and the sudden pressure spike caused a rupture at a corroded girth weld located 0.6 mi downstream of the station. approximately 420 mmcf of natural gas ignited, producing a flame extending 120 ft. the incident triggered an automatic shutdown and was reported to the national response center (incident #2104875). investigation determined the primary cause was the technician's omission to confirm the valve lock-out status before re-pressurization. corrective actions included revising the lock-out/tag-out checklist, retraining all field personnel on valve verification procedures, and installing a secondary interlock on valve c-9 to prevent inadvertent opening during maintenance. the line was repaired and returned to service on 23 november 2023 after hydrostatic testing at 1 300 psig.

NARRATIVE: on april 12, 2022 at 03:20 am the western interstate gas transmission company (wigtc) initiated a scheduled maintenance shutdown on line 44, a 30-inch carbon steel pipeline with a maop of 800 psig, located near the oakridge compression station. the work plan required the mainline isolation valve (ml-iv-12) to be placed in the automatic position after the pressure test so the emergency shutdown (esd) system could operate normally. however, the field supervisor mistakenly left ml-iv-12 in the manual position and failed to reinstall the temporary weep-hole plugs removed during the pressure test. at 04:05 am the esd system activated due to an upstream pressure surge; because the valve remained manual, it failed to close and gas continued to vent through the 36-inch downstream relief valve (rv-d-7). the vent persisted for approximately 45 minutes, releasing an estimated 4,200 mcf of natural gas, exceeding the 3,000 mcf reporting threshold. after the incident, an investigation identified a breakdown in the pre-job checklist verification and inadequate communication between the control center and field crew. corrective actions included revising the isolation valve reset procedure, adding a mandatory dual-sign-off on valve position, and installing a visual indicator to confirm automatic positioning of critical esd selectors.

NARRATIVE: on april 22, 2024, at approximately 06:45 local time, personnel at the midland mainline pump station began a routine restart of the 30-inch carbon steel transmission line after scheduled maintenance on the upstream metering skid. the station supervisor instructed the control room to close bypass valve b-12 and bring the line up to operating pressure of 850 psi. however, the field crew mistakenly opened relief valve r-3, which was intended only for emergency depressurization, and left the downstream isolation valve i-7 partially open. the pump unit 4-a was then started, rapidly increasing line pressure to 1,150 psi, exceeding the design limit of 1,000 psi for the 30-inch pipe. the over-pressure caused a longitudinal seam failure near milepost 42.7, releasing an estimated 4,200 bbl of crude oil and 650 mcf of natural gas into the surrounding wetland. the automatic shutdown system did not activate because the pressure transducer upstream of the failed section was disabled during the maintenance check. emergency response teams were dispatched within 12 minutes, and the leak was contained after 3.5 hours. investigation later determined that the incorrect valve configuration and failure to follow the standard operating procedure for valve sequencing were the primary contributors to the incident. corrective actions include revising the valve lockout-tagout protocol and reinstalling the disabled pressure transducer before resuming normal operations.

NARRATIVE: a maintenance crew was performing a valve replacement on a 24-inch carbon steel transmission line feeding the south field station. the line was rated for 850 psig but was being operated at 720 psig at the time of the work. the crew opened the downstream isolation valve without first verifying that the upstream valve was fully closed, assuming the line was depressurized after a recent pigging run. as the valve began to open, residual pressure surged forward, causing a sudden release of high-velocity natural gas. the escaping gas struck the crew member who was positioned on the valve stem, resulting in a flash fire that ignited a nearby oil-soaked rag. the employee suffered second-degree burns to the forearm and was taken to the regional trauma center. the incident also caused a 3-inch dent in the pipe wall and damaged the adjacent pressure regulator. the investigation found that the standard operating procedure for valve isolation was not followed, the pressure gauge was not cross-checked with the control system, and the required lockout/tagout steps were omitted. corrective actions included retraining all field personnel on proper isolation verification, updating the lockout/tagout checklist, and installing a secondary pressure monitoring point upstream of critical valve locations.

NARRATIVE: on september 14, 2022 a maintenance crew at the north ridge compression station was performing a scheduled pigging operation on the 24-inch, 1200-psi carbon-steel transmission line that serves the regional distribution grid. the work order called for the isolation of the line by closing the upstream manual isolation valve (miv-12) and the downstream automatic shut-off valve (asov-7) before inserting the pig. the crew, under pressure to finish before a scheduled night-time load increase, mistakenly closed the downstream asov-7 but left the upstream miv-12 partially open, assuming the valve had been locked out after a previous test. a supervisor, unaware of the incomplete lockout, gave the go-ahead signal to pressurize the line to normal operating pressure. as the compressor ramped up to 1100 psi, gas began escaping through the partially seated miv-12 stem, creating a vapor cloud that drifted toward a nearby highway. the leak was not detected by the station's gas detection system because the sensor was calibrated for downstream locations. by the time the alarm was triggered, approximately 5.4 mmcf of natural gas had vented, prompting an emergency shut-down and evacuation of the surrounding area. post-incident review identified a breakdown in lockout/tagout compliance and a lack of verification of valve positions before restart.

NARRATIVE: on november 3, 2025, at approximately 0715 hours, a kansas gas transmission services crew began routine maintenance on a 12-inch api 5l seamless steel main (schedule 40) located at the willow ridge pump station, segment b-12. the task involved removing the hydraulic hand-pump from the 500-psi rated valve 27-b, a 28-inch dual-acting gate valve that had been scheduled for replacement due to corrosion at the stem packing. after disconnecting the existing hand-pump, the technician mistakenly attached a 750-psi rated pneumatic actuator that had been left in the tool kit from a previous job. without verifying the actuator's pressure rating or consulting the manufacturer's operating procedure, the crew engaged the actuator to close the valve. the over-pressurized actuation caused the valve seat to shear, allowing high-pressure natural gas (approximately 820 psig) to surge into the downstream isolation line, which was still depressurized for the work. the sudden pressure spike ruptured a 6-inch tie-in fitting, resulting in an immediate release of gas and a flash fire that injured two crew members (second-degree burns) and ignited nearby vegetation. emergency shutdown was initiated at 0723 hours, and the affected segment was isolated and later repaired. the incident was reported to the nrc (nrc# 1089321) and the cpuc within the required reporting window.

NARRATIVE: on 04/17/2022 at 14:22 cd t, the riverbend compression station observed an unexpected pressure rise in the 24-inch mainline feeding the #2 gas turbine. the field operator, responding to a low-flow alarm, manually opened the downstream isolation valve (isolation valve-b) to increase flow, unaware that the upstream safety shutdown valve (ssv-a) had already been tripped due to a high-pressure condition at 1 250 psig (design limit 1 200 psig). the operator's action caused the ssv-a to remain closed while the isolation valve-b stayed open, resulting in a rapid pressure buildup to 1 380 psig downstream of the turbine inlet. the turbine's protective shutdown did not engage because the pressure sensor on the turbine inlet was reading the upstream pressure, which was still below its setpoint. after approximately 7 minutes, the over-pressurization forced the turbine inlet safety valve to lift, venting natural gas to the atmosphere through the flare stack. the incident was reported to the nrc at 15:05 cd t (report no. 2479135). investigation revealed that the operator misinterpreted the low-flow alarm and failed to verify the status of ssv-a in the control room display, which incorrectly showed the valve as closed due to a stuck limit-switch. corrective actions included installing a secondary visual indicator for ssv-a position, revising the low-flow alarm procedure to require verification of upstream valve status, and retraining all station personnel on valve interlocks. supplemental report filed 04/20/2022 updated the root cause to operator error during manual valve operation and corrected the initial nrc report date.

NARRATIVE: on april 12, 2024, a maintenance crew was performing a scheduled valve replacement on the western intertie 30-inch carbon steel mainline (api 5l grade b) near the silver creek junction in montana. the line was operating at 850 psig, well below its 1200 psig maximum allowable operating pressure. technicians removed the existing block-down valve and installed a new double-seal butterfly valve. the installation procedure required the use of a calibrated torque wrench and the application of moly-based lubricant to all bolt threads prior to final tightening, as specified in the company's valve-installation standard (procedure p-v12). however, due to a rushed shift change, the crew relied on a handheld torque indicator that was not calibrated and omitted the lubricant step. after the valve was hand-tightened, the line was repressurized to 850 psig without a leak check. within minutes, a low-frequency vibration was heard, and a faint odor of natural gas was reported by a nearby landowner. the valve seat failed, allowing a release of approximately 2,200 mcf of gas before the automatic shutdown system isolated the segment at 9:18 am. emergency response teams erected a safety perimeter, evacuated two nearby farms, and initiated a controlled blow-down to zero pressure. investigation later determined that the improper torque application and missing lubricant caused uneven bolt preload, leading to seat deformation and gasket failure. corrective actions included retraining on torque verification, mandatory calibration logs for torque tools, and revision of the valve-installation procedure to require a documented torque-recording step and verified lubrication before each installation.
