NARRATIVE: on april 22, 2024 at 07:45 a.m. the ridgeview gas processing facility initiated a scheduled pigging run on the 24-inch mainline that transports raw natural gas from the west field to the east processing unit. the operations crew opened the pig launcher valve and set the launch pressure to 350 psi, which was the standard for a 30-inch pipe but exceeded the 24-inch line's maximum allowable launch pressure of 300 psi. the pig entered the line and began moving toward the downstream pig catcher. however, because the launch pressure was too high, the pig's speed increased to approximately 12 ft/s, causing it to strike a recently installed 3-inch bypass valve that was still partially open for maintenance. the impact forced the bypass valve to close abruptly, creating a pressure surge that traveled back toward the launch site. the surge caused the upstream isolation valve to fail to close, and the control system recorded a closed-valve status even though the valve remained partially open. gas escaped through the isolation valve seat for about 45 minutes, resulting in an estimated loss of 6.2 mmcf. the incident was reported to the nrc at 13:20. investigation revealed that the operator had referenced the wrong line specifications in the pigging procedure checklist. corrective actions included revising the pig launch pressure limits for all pipe sizes, implementing a double-check verification step in the electronic work order system, and retraining the crew on line-size specific parameters. the bypass valve was inspected, repaired, and a pressure-relief bypass was installed to prevent future surges.

NARRATIVE: on october 12, 2023, a 6-inch x 24-inch pig launcher at the midstream compressor station experienced an unintended release of natural gas during routine maintenance. the vessel was connected to an 8-inch x 26-inch transmission line segment with a max allowable operating pressure (maop) of 1,000 psig, but the line was currently operating at approximately 650 psig. the relief valve on the pig launcher was set at 700 psig to protect the gauge and skid equipment. during the changeout of a faulty pressure transducer, field technicians failed to isolate the vessel from the main supply header via the existing 2-inch shutoff valve. instead, they assumed the valve was blocked in due to a tag on the handle from a previous unrelated ticket. when the gas control room received a request to boost pressure for downstream demand, they increased the line pressure to 850 psig without verifying the isolation status of the maintenance branch. this sudden pressure surge exceeded the 700 psig set point of the relief valve, causing it to lift and vent approximately 2.5 mmcf of gas to the atmosphere over a 45-minute period until the field crew isolated the valve and notified control. no injuries occurred, and the area was deemed safe after toxicity testing. the investigation determined that the root cause was a failure to verify the actual isolation status of equipment prior to energizing the pipeline, compounded by a lack of real-time communication between field operations and the control room regarding the specific maintenance activity and the conservative pressure settings established for the work scope.

NARRATIVE: on march 12, 2022, a contractor crew performing hot-tap operations on a 24-inch, 60-pound x65 pipe segment at milepost 42.5 experienced an uncontrolled gas release. at 14:00 hrs, the crew initiated the cutting process using an electric boom saw. during the procedure, the operator adjusted the feed rate controller incorrectly, causing the saw to apply excessive downward pressure on the pipe wall rather than allowing the rotation to perform the cut. this misoperation resulted in the cut depth exceeding the allowable limit for hot-tapping, penetrating the entire pipe wall and creating a full-bore release. the resulting hole measured approximately 0.5 inches in diameter, and an estimated 850 mcf of natural gas was vented to the atmosphere before the emergency shutdown device (esd) actuated at 14:04 hrs. the crew immediately evacuated the immediate work area to a safe distance and monitored the surrounding area for potential ignition sources. following the event, an internal review determined that the cause was the operator's failure to calibrate the feed rate mechanism prior to commencing the cut, a specific requirement detailed in the in-service repair procedure manual. the operator had not completed the advanced in-service repair training required for diameters exceeding 20 inches. subsequent root cause analysis identified that the work permit was issued without verifying the specific competency of the individual operating the equipment. corrective actions included mandatory retraining for all hot-tap operators and the implementation of a dual-verification step for feed rate settings before tool engagement. the pipeline segment was repair patched and returned to service on march 15, 2022, after passing all required in-line inspection and pressure testing requirements.

NARRATIVE: on october 14, 2021, at approximately 0930 hours, an incident occurred at the pines cross-country compressor facility during planned maintenance on the discharge station piping. personnel were executing the replacement of a failed 24-inch full-bore ball valve on the main suction line, operating under a type a hot work permit. the line was isolated using remote-operated gate valves and depressurized to atmospheric levels. during the initial break-bolt process, a residual pressure spike was observed on the local gauge, indicating that a downstream check valve had failed to seat properly against the isolation boundary. before the field team could fully locate the true source of the residual flow, a manual bleed valve was opened to equalize pressure, resulting in a rapid release of unaccounted-for natural gas. the sudden release created a sonic jet that struck a maintenance technician standing within the defined exclusion zone. the individual suffered minor thermal burns to the forearms due to the rapid expansion of the gas. emergency services were dispatched immediately, and the employee was transported to the regional medical center for monitoring and treatment. subsequent investigation revealed that the blowdown procedure did not adequately account for the failure mode of the inline check valve, and the operational team proceeded with the line cut without verifying zero energy state via multiple independent indicators. phmsa was notified of the incident per regulatory requirements. corrective actions included mandatory retraining on isolation verification procedures and the implementation of additional mechanical locking devices on critical isolation points.

NARRATIVE: on february 14, 2022, a 12-inch transmission line operated by gaspy-49 pipeline corporation, llc (company) experienced a partial release at a valve operating station in trinity county, east texas. the incident occurred during the reconfiguration of the segment feedercamp loop to transfer right of way assets from the company to a third-party operator. maintenance crew members were tasked with closing the mainline valve and opening a previously isolated tie-in valve to bypass the section. according to the task order, the tie-in valve was to remain in the manual position during the pressure test phase. however, field personnel mistakenly engaged the pneumatic actuator of the tie-in valve before the mainline pressure had been sufficiently reduced. this action caused the valve to travel rapidly against a significant backpressure differential, approximately 450 psig, resulting in a sudden surge of force transmitted through the 20-inch api 5l x65 pipe welds. the hydraulic shock overwhelmed the gasket seal on an adjacent branch connection, leading to a high-velocity gas release. the event triggered the station's automatic emergency shutdown (esd) system, which isolated the affected segment within 30 seconds. no injuries were reported. post-incident review revealed that the crew had deviated from the standard operating procedure by releasing the pneumatic air supply lockout tag before verifying zero line pressure. the company has since implemented a mandatory two-person verification protocol for actuator engagements and updated their control room software to interlock pneumatic operations with upstream pressure transmitters to prevent similar misoperations.

NARRATIVE: on july 14, 2024, a maintenance crew was performing routine inspection on a 24-inch nominal diameter type i steel pipeline operating at 625 psig. the workflow involved the hydrostatic testing of a newly installed pig launcher located at mile marker 42. the site supervisor authorized the operation after confirming that the upstream isolation valves were in the closed position and locked out. however, during the filling phase, a shift change occurred, and the incoming technician mistakenly believed the manual gate valve at the bottom of the launcher was fully open when it was actually in a half-open position. the technicians commenced high-pressure water injection using a portable pump rated for 1,500 psig. because the drain line was not properly purged, the restricted flow caused a rapid pressure spike within the confined space of the launcher hull. at approximately 10:45 am, the internal gauge registered a dangerous exceedance of 950 psig. the crew member manning the pump failed to monitor the secondary pressure indicator mounted on the remote manifold, relying solely on the primary gauge which had a broken needle. within two minutes, the 6061-t aluminum flange on the launcher failed, causing a catastrophic rupture. high-velocity water and debris escaped, damaging adjacent low-carbon steel piping and deploying safety netting. no personnel were injured as the crew was positioned outside the designated exclusion zone. the investigation determined that the root cause was the incorrect execution of the pre-operation checklist, specifically the failure to verify valve position and the inadequacy of pressure monitoring procedures during the hydrotest. corrective actions included implementing a dual-verification protocol for valve positions and installing automatic pressure relief alarms on all portable testing units.

NARRATIVE: on 11/12/2023 at 14:45, operators at the ridgeline station reported a sudden drop in suction pressure on the 24-inch gas line. the primary compressor train was operating at 62% load with a discharge pressure of 980 psig. in an effort to balance the system load following a downstream reduction at the northfield junction, the shift supervisor instructed the operator to open the bypass manual gate valve around the automatic control valve. the operator misidentified the valve configuration due to poor lighting in the battery room and fully opened the maintenance isolation valve instead of the slow-opening bypass. this action created a short circuit, causing approximately 4,500 mcf/hr of gas to bypass the metering skid and flow directly into the storage field. the system pressure rapidly declined to 30 psig below the minimum operating limit, triggering a low-pressure alarm on the central control system. simultaneously, the unregulated flow caused vibration in the downstream 10-inch lateral line, leading to minor seal leakage at the flanged connection near the pigging launcher. field personnel were dispatched to the site at 15:20, where the abnormal flow sound confirmed the bypass had been opened. they immediately closed the offending valve and restored normal operations by 15:45. investigation revealed that the valve tags were faded and the specific bypass procedure required the use of a torque wrench to prevent over-tightening or misalignment. the incident was attributed to the operator selecting the wrong valve assembly during a high-stress manual intervention. corrective actions include replacing all valve tags with high-visibility color coding, installing mechanical locking devices to prevent accidental full-open positions, and implementing mandatory spot-check protocols before executing bypass maneuvers on critical flow control lines.

NARRATIVE: on 03/14/2022, a natural gas release occurred at the red rock compressor station during routine maintenance activities. at approximately 10:15 am, a maintenance technician was tasked with isolating the 12-inch inlet piping for compressor unit 3 to replace a flange gasket. the technician manually operated the quarter-turn ball valve shut-off, believing the handwheel was tight against the stop due to corrosion buildup on the stem. verification via the local local supervisory control and data acquisition panel showed the valve status indicator reporting "closed," but this signal was delayed due to a known limiter fault that had not been cleared. when the isolation flange was broken, pressurized gas at approximately 850 psig was immediately released from the downstream segment, creating a significant jet of gas that ignited upon contact with a hot surface from a nearby exhaust manifold. operations were notified at 10:17 am and performed an emergency shutdown of the station at 10:19 am, limiting the total release to an estimated 4,200 mscf. post-incident inspection revealed the ball valve seat was only partially seated, allowing flow through the centerline. the facility subsequently updated its operating procedures to require physical position verification via gauging rods for all critical isolation valves before breaking flanges, and installed mechanical limiters on all existing ball valves to prevent over-torquing.

NARRATIVE: during a scheduled maintenance window on the north field gathering line, field technicians were tasked with isolating a 12-inch carbon steel segment for hydrostatic testing. standard procedure required closing two 6-inch gate valves at the segment ends and verifying low pressure via the local gauges. however, the lead technician observed a slight pressure reading on the downstream gauge and, without consulting the revised piping and instrumentation layout, assumed the downstream valve had failed to seat properly. lacking a direct bleed line access at that location, the technician decided to manually purge the line through a nearby 2-inch sample point to force the downstream gauge to zero. this action was not authorized by the shift supervisor and bypassed the required secondary isolation check. as the sample valve was opened, unknown high-pressure fluid, later identified as 14-inch diesel fuel from an adjacent parallel header, surged into the isolated low-pressure natural gas section. the sudden pressure differential exceeded the design rating of the sample tubing, causing the flexible pipe to rupture. the resulting spray of fuel created an ignitable cloud near an active electrical enclosure on the skid. although the station eir quickly tripped due to gas detection, the initial mechanical failure and safety violation constituted an operational error. the incident resulted in minor scarring to the skid frame and a 45-minute shutdown while the misrouted sample line was replaced and hydrotested.

NARRATIVE: on 03/14/2023 at 14:45, a technician at the harper field compressor station was performing routine maintenance on the unit lube oil filtration system. while replacing the upstream 2-inch strainer, the technician failed to prioritize the lockout tagout procedure for the 8-inch polyethylene suction line connected to the skid. the line was currently delivering 14.5 mmcf at 600 psig. upon removing the last retaining bolt, the valve handle on the adjacent 6-inch stainless steel isolation valve was inadvertently bumped, rotating it 90 degrees from the open position to closed. this action isolated the lube oil pump and caused a rapid pressure drop in the hydraulic accumulator bank. the resulting loss of hydraulic pressure triggered an unplanned trip of the compressor unit. simultaneously, the sudden closure of the isolation valve created a transient pressure surge in the downstream 4-inch carbon steel discharge header, reaching 650 psig, which activated the high-pressure interlock. the emergency shutdown sequence automatically opened the automatic vent valve, releasing approximately 12,000 scf of hydrocarbon vapor into the flare system. field operations responded to secure the area and verify line integrity. after inspection, no mechanical damage to the piping was observed. the isolated valve was manually reopened to restore normal flow. the incident was attributed to the technician incorrectly positioning the valve stem access panel, which obstructed the operating handle, leading to accidental actuation during the strainer removal process. corrective actions included installing a protective guard over the valve handle and revising the maintenance procedure to mandate visual confirmation of valve position before and after all upstream line operations.

NARRATIVE: on october 14, 2019, a maintenance crew was performing routine inspection and lubrication of the pneumatic actuator on a 24-inch diameter 600 psi transmission line gate valve at kilometre 45. the operator, following a standard work permit, intended to manually override the actuator to cycle the valve stem for maintenance verification. however, the operator failed to properly secure the manual override loop and engaged the hydraulic power unit while the main supply line remained fully pressurized at 580 psi. upon engagement, the unsecured linkage snapped and the valve stem rotated fully closed in less than two seconds without the required gradual sequencing. this sudden closure caused a severe pressure surge in the upstream section of the pipeline, triggering the high-pressure alarm and automatic shutdown sequence in control room. the abrupt shut-in resulted in a temporary loss of transmission service for approximately 45 minutes, disrupting flow to a major compressor station downstream. no personal injuries or gas releases were reported. the investigation revealed that the operator had not completed the mandatory pre-operation checklist verifying the isolation of the hydraulic power source. additionally, the physical guard designed to prevent manual override engagement while under load was found to be damaged and non-functional. the operator's qualification for operating critical safety protection systems was suspended pending retraining. the valve and hydraulic system were repaired, tested, and returned to service on october 16, 2019. corrective actions included replacing the damaged guard, revising the procedural lockout/tagout requirements, and implementing a new digital verification step in the work management system to ensure power sources are confirmed de-energized before manual interventions.

NARRATIVE: at 06:45 hours on november 12, 2023, a line isolation valve (liv) failed to close during a planned maintenance window at the red haw consolidation point. two operators were performing a routine blowdown of pipeline segment 45-78, a 36-inch diameter x 0.375-inch wall, api 5l x65 pipe. the objective was to reduce the line pressure from 850 psig to less than 50 psig to allow safe removal of a leaking gate valve. according to the work order, the upiside liv was to be closed first, followed by the downiside liv, before opening the manual blowdown valve. the field crew initially closed the downiside liv but accidentally left the upiside liv in the open position due to a visual confirmation error caused by heavy fog accumulation on the control valve position indicator. subsequently, the manual blowdown valve was opened, causing uncontrolled depressurization from the upstream segment connected to the main transmission line. this action released approximately 1,200 mmcf of natural gas into the atmosphere through the vent stack at a rate of 4.5 dscfh for nearly three hours before the pressure drop in the upstream segment was detected by the scada system. the upstream liv was manually closed via the remote panel, halting the release. an internal review determined that the confusion between lever positions on the actuator head, combined with the lack of a witness check by the lead operator, resulted in the sequence error. no injuries were reported, but the incident triggered a station-wide alarm. corrective actions included the installation of distinct color-coding on valve handles and mandatory two-person verification steps for all isolation operations during low-visibility conditions.
